claims.claim: The study notes Martin's conspicuous use of the archaic native prefix a- for position, in atop, abed and ahorse.
claims.source: Simon, 'Affixes, compound and combination words', Books & Boots
claims.quote: he conspicuously deploys the archaic prefix

claims.claim: The study concludes that Martin's lexical choices matter as much as his subject matter in producing the novels' archaic worldview.
claims.source: Simon, 'Affixes, compound and combination words', Books & Boots
claims.quote: the lexical choices he makes are as important as the subject matter

claims.claim: The essayist characterises Martin's narration as a steady flow of low-density sentences that keeps pages turning.
claims.source: At Sea Journal, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer'
claims.quote: Martin keeps us turning pages with a steady flow of low-density sentences
claims.page: section on oral versus textual storytelling

claims.claim: The essayist calls the method shotgun writing, in which no single sentence carries the effect on its own.
claims.source: At Sea Journal, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer'
claims.quote: It’s shotgun writing: like buckshot, no single sentence is that effective
claims.page: section on oral versus textual storytelling

claims.claim: The essayist puts the non-dialogue share of the text at 60 percent and calls that prose forgettable.
claims.source: At Sea Journal, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer'
claims.quote: the prose that constitutes the other 60% of the text is forgettable
claims.page: section 'The con: The sentences aren't beautiful'

claims.claim: The essayist argues stock phrases persist because they come easily to a writer working for flow.
claims.source: At Sea Journal, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer'
claims.quote: for a writer, they come easily off the pen

claims.claim: The author of the five-part video series on Martin's prose credits him with knowing where to end a sentence inside a long description.
claims.source: Corey Huffman, video description, '[1] The Prose of George R R Martin | How to Write Focused Descriptions'
claims.quote: Martin knows just where to drop his periods

claims.claim: The same video's description says Martin breaks large descriptions into easily digestible sentences.
claims.source: Corey Huffman, video description, '[1] The Prose of George R R Martin'
claims.quote: break up large descriptions into easily digestible sentences

claims.claim: Part two of the series treats contrast as the technique that lets one Martin description do several narrative jobs at once.
claims.source: Corey Huffman, video description, '[2] The Prose of George R R Martin | Why You Should Contrast Your Descriptions'
claims.quote: how Martin uses the literary technique of “contrast” to enrich these descriptions

claims.claim: Part three of the series examines twenty-five metaphors and similes drawn from A Game of Thrones.
claims.source: Corey Huffman, video description, '[3] The Prose of George R R Martin | Masterful Metaphors & Similes'
claims.quote: I examine twenty-five metaphors and similes masterfully crafted by George R R

claims.claim: Part four claims Martin frequently structures adjectives, nouns and clauses in threes.
claims.source: Corey Huffman, video description, '[4] The Prose of George R R Martin | Adjectives & The Rule of 3'
claims.quote: he often uses "The Rule of 3" with regards to structuring

claims.claim: Part five uses passages from A Clash of Kings to argue Martin melds active and passive voice within a single narrative movement.
claims.source: Corey Huffman, video description, '[5] The Prose of George R R Martin | How to Meld the Active & Passive Voices'
claims.quote: how to differentiate between the Active and Passive voices

claims.claim: The reviewer prefers Martin's vampire history to Anne Rice's because of what Martin leaves unsaid.
claims.source: Rob H. Bedford, review of Fevre Dream, SFFWorld
claims.quote: more successful than Rice’s history more for what is left unsaid

claims.claim: Adam Whitehead judges The Mystery Knight to lack the elegant simplicity of The Hedge Knight.
claims.source: Adam Whitehead (Werthead), review posted in the Malazan Empire thread 'The Tales of Dunk and Egg'
claims.quote: It lacks the elegant simplicity of The Hedge Knight
claims.page: The Mystery Knight review, quoted post

claims.claim: The same reviewer says the novella's ending is unusually neat for Martin and lacks the messy consequences he usually favours.
claims.source: Adam Whitehead (Werthead), review posted in the Malazan Empire thread 'The Tales of Dunk and Egg'
claims.quote: lacks the messy consequences he usually favours
claims.page: The Mystery Knight review, quoted post
